newsitem.title: FRANCE: Car sales in France fell 21.7 percent in November.
newsitem.headline: Car sales in France fell 21.7 percent in November.

text.p: New car sales in France fell 21.7 percent in November as demand dried up after a summer buying spree, the French carmakers' association CCFA said on Monday.
New car registrations slid to 135,294 from 172,849 last November, which was already nine percent below 1994 levels.

CCFA spokesman Jean-Claude Nicolas told a news conference that two factors accounted for the decline. "The end of a (year-long) state rebate scheme in September had the customary effect of pulling sales forward from the months that follow," he said.
In September, the last month in which the rebates were available, car sales in France rocketed 86 percent.
"In addition, there were fewer working days in November -- 19 compared with 21 in November 1995," Nicolas said. On a comparable working day basis, November car sales were down 13.5 percent.
A disruptive 12-day truckers' strike last month also dented November sales and is expected to result in "a sad month for December", CCFA chairman Henry Streit told the conference.
For the first 11 months of the year, car sales totalled 1.99 million -- up 11.2 percent from the same period a year earlier and ahead of the 1995 full-year total of 1.92 million.
Streit also said the CCFA would not give a forecast for 1996 because of the effects of the strike, adding that the strike was likely to have "greater consequences" than media had reported.
For the year to November, the French carmakers' share of the market shrank to 56.1 percent from 60 percent, while foreign carmakers increased their share to 43.9 percent from 40 percent.

Streit said foreign carmakers which have shifted production to countries with weak currencies such as Britain, Spain and Italy have developed a big competitive advantage over French companies in terms of production costs.
Opel, the German-based subsidiary of General Motors, produces only 30 percent of its cars in Germany, and Volkswagen produces only 42 to 43 percent in its home market.
In contrast, French carmakers PSA Peugeot Citroen and Renault SA produce three-quarters of their cars in France.
The Peugeot group's car sales in France fell 27 percent in November, while Renault's sales fell 20.4 percent.
Volkswagen car sales rose 11.7 percent, GM sales rose 6.4 percent, Ford sales climbed 7.6 percent, Fiat sales rose eight percent, and sales of Japanese cars rose 3.8 percent last month in France.

CCFA figures for the first 10 months of the year confirmed that the rebate plan steered sales toward less expensive models. Sales of small and compact cars accounted for 73.8 percent of the total, up from 71.7 percent in the first 10 months of 1995.

The rebate plan also altered the ratio of new car sales to used car sales, with new car sales gaining the edge. The ratio was 1.8 to one in the first 10 months of 1996, compared with 2.1 to one in all of 1995 and 2.5 to one for 1993.

French car exports rose 3.9 percent in the first 10 months of 1996, with sales climbing in the three biggest markets, Britain, Spain and Germany, but falling in fourth-ranked Italy. The top-selling French export was Renault's Megane, followed by the Peugeot 306 and the Renault Clio.
